passages.t: At Shechem: the story told with God as its subject
passages.happening:
Joshua gathers all the tribes at Shechem. The elders, leaders, judges and officers come, ‘and they presented themselves before God’ (verse 1).

He speaks in God's name: ‘This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says’. And God tells Israel its own story.

It begins before Abraham. ‘Long ago your fathers, including Terah the father of Abraham and Nahor, lived beyond the Euphrates and worshiped other gods’ (verse 2). ‘But I took your father Abraham from beyond the Euphrates and led him through all the land of Canaan, and I multiplied his descendants’ (verse 3). God gave him Isaac, and to Isaac he gave Jacob and Esau. Jacob and his sons went down to Egypt.

‘Then I sent Moses and Aaron, and I afflicted the Egyptians by what I did there, and afterward I brought you out’ (verse 5). God recalls the sea, the long years in the wilderness, the kings east of the Jordan, and Balaam, whose curse he would not hear. Then the crossing, and Jericho, and the peoples of the land.

The story ends with a gift. ‘So I gave you a land on which you did not toil and cities that you did not build, and now you live in them and eat from vineyards and olive groves that you did not plant’ (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
Shechem was the right place for this. It lay between Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim, in the middle of the land. Abraham had built his first altar in Canaan there, when God first told him that this land would belong to his descendants. Jacob had bought a field there, and there his household had buried the foreign gods they had been carrying. Joshua had already read the law to Israel between the two mountains. Now, at the end of his life, he brings the people back to where the promise began.

The speech has a surprising first line. Israel's story does not begin with a good man who sought God. It begins with a family across the Euphrates that ‘worshiped other gods’. Abraham's own father was one of them. Israel is being told that it has no noble origin to be proud of. It began among idols, and God took it from there.

A reader should watch the verbs: ‘I took’, ‘I gave’, ‘I sent’, ‘I brought you out’, ‘I delivered’, ‘I gave’. From the first line to the last, God is the one who acts, and Israel is the one who receives. Even the battles are told that way. The victory came, God says, ‘but not by your own sword or bow’ (verse 12).

Since the 1950s many scholars have compared this chapter with treaties made between great kings and lesser kings in the ancient world, above all those of the Hittites. Those treaties usually began by naming the great king and telling what he had done for the lesser king. Only then did they set out what loyalty required. They called witnesses and provided for a written copy. Joshua 24 has the same parts: a history, a call for loyalty, witnesses and a written record. How close the likeness is, and what it shows about when the chapter was written, is debated. But it helps a reader to see that this is a covenant ceremony, and that in such a ceremony the kindness of the king comes before the duty of the people.

The last sentence gathers the whole book. Israel lives in cities it did not build and eats from vines it did not plant. The land is not a wage. It is a gift.
passages.later:
Moses had described this gift before Israel entered: ‘a land with great and splendid cities that you did not build’ (Deuteronomy 6:10).

Stephen, in the book of Acts, tells the same story from the same starting point: “The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham while he was still in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran” (Acts 7:2).

Paul uses Abraham to make the point this chapter makes about beginnings: God is the one ‘who justifies the wicked’ (Romans 4:5).
passages.asks: God told Israel its story with himself as the subject of every sentence. Try telling your own story that way: where he found you, what he gave, where he brought you out. Ask what changes when you are not the hero of it. And think about the first line. Ask whether you believe that God begins with people where they are, among whatever gods their families served.

passages.t: ‘Choose for yourselves this day whom you will serve’
passages.happening:
Now Joshua speaks for himself. “Now, therefore, fear the LORD and serve Him in sincerity and truth; cast aside the gods your fathers served beyond the Euphrates and in Egypt, and serve the LORD” (verse 14).

Then he puts the matter as a choice. “But if it is unpleasing in your sight to serve the LORD, then choose for yourselves this day whom you will serve, whether the gods your fathers served beyond the Euphrates, or the gods of the Amorites in whose land you are living. As for me and my house, we will serve the LORD!” (verse 15).

The people answer at once. “Far be it from us to forsake the LORD to serve other gods!” (verse 16). They give their reasons, and their reasons are the story they have just heard. The LORD brought them and their fathers out of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. He did great signs before their eyes. He protected them on the way and drove out the nations before them. ‘We too will serve the LORD, because He is our God’ (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
The first two words matter most: ‘Now, therefore’. Everything Joshua asks rests on the thirteen verses before it. God took, gave, sent, brought out and gave again. Therefore serve him. The order is the order of the whole Bible. God acts first, and the call to serve him is an answer to what he has done.

The word ‘serve’ runs all through this chapter. In Hebrew one word covers the work of a slave, the loyalty owed to a king, and the worship of a god. Israel had served Pharaoh, and God brought it out of ‘the house of slavery’. Joshua's speech assumes that everyone serves something. The only question is what.

Verse 14 admits something uncomfortable. Joshua tells the people to ‘cast aside’ the gods of their fathers. So some of them still had such gods. After the Jordan, Jericho and the gift of the land, there were images from Mesopotamia and Egypt among Israel's belongings. In that world it was normal to honor many gods. To serve one alone was the strange demand.

Then comes the famous sentence, and it has to be read as it stands. Joshua does not offer a choice between the LORD and nothing. He says: if you will not serve the LORD, then choose which of the other gods you want, the old ones from beyond the river or the local ones of Canaan. There is an edge of irony in it. He lays out the alternatives so that the people can see them for what they are.

It is also worth seeing whom he is speaking to. These are not strangers who have never heard of God. They are his own covenant people, standing in a land he gave them, at a ceremony to renew a bond he made. The choice is whether they will be loyal to the God who has already made them his.

Joshua does not wait to see how the vote goes. ‘As for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.’ He speaks for himself and his own household, whatever the rest decide. He is an old man with nothing to gain, saying where he stands.

The people's answer is good, and it is good for the right reason. They do not say they will serve God because they are afraid, or because Joshua has told them to. They repeat what God has done.
passages.later:
Moses had put the same kind of choice before the generation that was about to enter the land: “I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing. Therefore choose life, so that you and your descendants may live” (Deuteronomy 30:19).

Jesus said that no one can avoid serving something: “No one can serve two masters: Either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve both God and money” (Matthew 6:24).
passages.hard:
Is ‘choose for yourselves this day’ a demand that the reader decide for God on the spot?

The sentence is often quoted that way, lifted out of its chapter and used to press people for a decision. In its own setting it is something else.

It is spoken to a people who already belong to God. He chose Abraham, brought them out of Egypt, and gave them the land. The ceremony is the renewing of a covenant that God made first. The Hebrew word for ‘choose’ is often used in the Old Testament of God choosing Israel. Joshua's call does not mean that God's choice waits on theirs. It calls them to answer his choice with their own.

It comes after thirteen verses of what God has done, and it rests on them.

And Joshua does not rush the people. When they say yes, his next words slow them down and tell them how serious it is (verse 19).

So the verse gives no one a tool for pressure. No preacher, parent or friend is given the right to corner another person with it. What it does is ask a real question of people who have received much from God: now that you know what he has done, whom will you serve? That question is worth taking time over, and God is patient with those who take it seriously.
passages.asks: Joshua said ‘therefore’ and pointed back to everything God had done. Before asking what you will do for God, go back over what he has done for you. Then ask what you are in fact serving, the thing your time, money and worry actually go to. And notice that Joshua spoke for his own house without waiting for the crowd. Ask where you are waiting to see what others decide.

passages.t: ‘You are not able to serve the LORD’
passages.happening:
The people have said yes, and Joshua's reply is the last thing anyone expects. “You are not able to serve the LORD, for He is a holy God; He is a jealous God; He will not forgive your rebellion or your sins. If you forsake the LORD and serve foreign gods, He will turn and bring disaster on you and consume you, even after He has been good to you” (verses 19-20).

The people insist: ‘We will serve the LORD’ (verse 21).

Joshua says, “You are witnesses against yourselves that you have chosen to serve the LORD.” They agree: ‘We are witnesses’ (verse 22).

Then he tells them to act on it. “Now, therefore,” he said, “get rid of the foreign gods among you and incline your hearts to the LORD, the God of Israel” (verse 23). A third time they promise: “We will serve the LORD our God and obey His voice” (verse 24).

That day Joshua makes a covenant for the people at Shechem. He writes these things in the Book of the Law of God. He takes a large stone and sets it up under the oak by the sanctuary of the LORD, and says, “You see this stone. It will be a witness against us, for it has heard all the words the LORD has spoken to us” (verse 27). Then he sends everyone home.
passages.hearers:
Most leaders who had just won a promise of loyalty would have thanked the people and closed the meeting. Joshua tells them they cannot do what they have promised.

He is not trying to drive them off. He is testing whether they know what they are saying. A promise made lightly is worth little, and Joshua knows this people. He has watched them for a lifetime. He wants them to count the cost before they bind themselves.

Two words describe the God they are promising to serve. ‘Holy’ means that he is wholly unlike the gods of the nations. He cannot be managed or kept in a corner of life beside other loyalties. ‘Jealous’ is a word the Old Testament uses only of God. It does not mean petty envy. It is the rightful claim of one who has given himself to a people and will not share them with rivals, as a husband or wife rightly expects faithfulness.

The words ‘He will not forgive’ are startling, and the hard question below takes them up. The next verse shows what Joshua has in view: a people who ‘forsake the LORD and serve foreign gods’.

The exchange goes back and forth three times, and each time the people's answer grows firmer. Joshua makes them hear themselves. They are witnesses against themselves. If they turn away later, no one will be able to say they did not know.

Then he asks for something they can do with their hands. If they mean it, the foreign gods have to go. Long before, on this same ground, Jacob's family had buried their foreign gods under the oak at Shechem.

The stone is the last of the book's memorials. There were twelve stones from the Jordan, a heap over Achan, the stones at the cave, and now this one. Joshua says the stone ‘has heard’. It is a vivid way to say that what was spoken here will stand. People forget. The stone will still be there.

Something is written down as well. Joshua records the covenant in ‘the Book of the Law of God’. The promise is given a fixed form that can be read to those not yet born.
passages.later:
The first commandment had already joined God's jealousy to his rescue of Israel: “You shall have no other gods before Me” (Exodus 20:3), ‘for I, the LORD your God, am a jealous God’ (Exodus 20:5).

The prophets saw that Joshua was right about Israel's inability, and they heard God promise to deal with it at the root: “I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts. And I will be their God, and they will be My people” (Jeremiah 31:33).

At his last supper Jesus took a cup and said, “This cup is the new covenant in My blood, which is poured out for you” (Luke 22:20).
passages.hard:
Why does Joshua say, ‘You are not able to serve the LORD’, and that God ‘will not forgive’? Does God not forgive sin?

Most readers take Joshua's words as a deliberate shock. The people have answered quickly, and he wants them to weigh what they are promising. He would sooner have a slow, sober yes than a quick one.

The words about forgiveness have to be read with the next verse. Joshua is speaking of people who ‘forsake the LORD and serve foreign gods’. He is warning against a settled turning away from God to other gods. He is not saying that God has no mercy for the sins his people fall into and bring to him. The same law of Moses that Joshua upheld gave Israel sacrifices for sin and described God as ‘forgiving iniquity, transgression, and sin’ (Exodus 34:7).

Some readers also hear plain realism in the words. Joshua knew Israel's record, and the book of Judges shows that he judged rightly.

Read with the rest of the Bible, the verse shows a need that the covenant at Shechem could not meet by itself. A people can promise sincerely and still fail. The prophets answered that need with God's promise to change the heart, and Christians believe that promise is kept in Christ.

These words must not be turned against the Jewish people, as if their story proved a special faithlessness. Joshua says ‘us’ in verse 27 and includes himself. The Bible tells Israel's failures because Israel's own teachers wrote them down, and every reader is meant to find himself in them.

The New Testament says to all who come back to God, “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).

If you are afraid that you have fallen away from God, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has. Read Romans 8:38-39 slowly. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Joshua would not accept an easy promise. Ask whether you have made promises to God quickly that you have not counted the cost of. Then ask what ‘foreign gods’ would have to be carried out of your house for your promise to be true. And hear the hard sentence honestly: you are not able. Ask whom you are relying on to make you able.

passages.happening:
“Some time later, Joshua son of Nun, the servant of the LORD, died at the age of 110” (verse 29). They bury him in his own town, Timnath-serah, in the hill country of Ephraim (verse 30).

The writer gives a verdict on his generation. “Israel had served the LORD throughout the days of Joshua and of the elders who outlived him and who had experienced all the works that the LORD had done for Israel” (verse 31).

A second burial follows. The bones of Joseph, which Israel had carried up out of Egypt, are buried at Shechem, in the piece of ground Jacob had bought long before (verse 32).

And a third. “Eleazar son of Aaron also died, and they buried him at Gibeah, which had been given to his son Phinehas in the hill country of Ephraim” (verse 33).
passages.hearers:
The book began with a death, ‘Moses My servant is dead’. It ends with three.

Joshua is given a title here for the first time. All through the book he has been ‘Joshua son of Nun’. Moses was ‘the servant of the LORD’. Only now, when his work is over, does the writer give Joshua the same name. He did not claim it. It was said of him afterward.

He died at 110, the age at which Joseph died. He was buried in the town he had asked for and rebuilt.

Verse 31 is high praise and a quiet warning. Israel served the LORD as long as Joshua lived, and as long as the elders lived who had seen what God did. The sentence stops there. It says nothing of the generation that had not seen. The next book opens with that generation.

Joseph's bones have been waiting for a very long time. When Joseph was dying in Egypt he made his brothers swear that when God brought them out, they would carry his bones with them. Moses took them at the exodus. They traveled through forty years of wilderness and all the years of this book. Now they are laid in the ground at Shechem, in the plot Jacob bought. Joseph had believed, in Egypt, that God would bring his people home. The burial shows that his trust was sound.

Eleazar was the son of Aaron and the high priest who had stood beside Joshua through the dividing of the land. With him the leaders of the entry are all gone.

So the last picture in the book is three graves, and every one of them is in the promised land. Abraham owned nothing in Canaan but a burial cave. These men are buried in ground their people hold as an inheritance. The promise that began with a grave bought from strangers ends, for now, with graves at home.

A reader may notice that the book's chief human figure ends as every person does. Joshua gave Israel rest, and then Joshua died. Whatever rest he gave could not be the last.
passages.later:
Joseph's request is in the last chapter of Genesis: “God will surely attend to you, and then you must carry my bones up from this place” (Genesis 50:25). Hebrews counts it as faith: “By faith Joseph, when his end was near, spoke about the exodus of the Israelites and gave instructions about his bones” (Hebrews 11:22).

The book of Judges begins by repeating verse 31 and then going on: “After that whole generation had also been gathered to their fathers, another generation rose up who did not know the LORD or the works that He had done for Israel” (Judges 2:10).

And Hebrews says what Joshua's death left open: “For if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken later about another day. There remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God” (Hebrews 4:8-9).
passages.asks: Israel was faithful as long as those who had seen God's works were alive. Ask what the people who come after you will know of God from you, when those who taught you are gone. Think of Joseph's bones, carried for generations on the strength of a promise. Ask what you are carrying in hope that you may not live to see. And ask where your own rest finally lies.
